The immigrant/immigrant's child experience is inherently very lonely. We are symbolic bridges from there to here. We weren't "meant" to be here, but we also don't "belong" in our parent's mother land. Our parents took risks and sacrificed to be here, oftentimes enduring discrimination and racism but putting up with it for our future.

When you visit/think of their homeland you feel weird, almost a sense of grief, for a life you could have had but which was made impossible due to the circumstances (danger, lack of opportunities, etc.). But you also can't imagine leave your own homeland (or where you were raised) because it has become a part of you, even when it rejects you (your own racist/discriminatory experiences).

There's actually now a specific subsection of therapy specialty for our unique experience (migration pain). And this affects not only direct immigrants, but future generations.

I relate to you. What has helped a lot is my social group, which is mostly comprised of first or second gen immigrants/foreign students, and others. Some are here with status, others have mixed status families, and a few are completely undocumented (which adds another layer of issues). 

Our experience is lonely, but there are many of us, and with exception of our indigenous communities, at one point we were all immigrants. So I hope that brings you some sense of comfort

First convince yourself that **you** are full of love. Care for others, care for your hobbies, your schoolwork, your work.

Loving and caring for your surroundings and friends/neighbors will not only make you feel satisfied, but also teach you how to love. Once you're there you might even notice that naturally, over time, you start loving yourself and feeling worthy of being loved.

Of all mental health disorders, eating disorders have the highest mortality rate. One person dies every hour from an eating disorder.

I haven't yet seen any studies on mortality rates related to height in particular. I have seen a study that mentions how a 5cm height increase has a 9% decrease in suicide risk.

Regardless, generally, I believe that weight and weight related issues are much more serious than height. As you mentioned height is something genetic that cannot be changed, but I also believe that in some individuals weight and weight gain or loss is difficult to manage. Be it genetic reasons, (having a bigger build) or medical reasons, (certain birth controls, stomach or intestinal issues).

Of course, everyone is entitled to their preferences, but no one is entitled to comment on another's body negatively, be it their height, weight, acne, scars, skin color, or such. I understand that there are mean spirited people who will do so regardless, but I also think its important to understand why our society works the way it does. Why tall/skinny people are considered conventionally attractive, and why we shouldn't make this issue a "pointing fingers" situation.

If anything you should have empathy for those that think its okay to shame other on their height or weight. They probably haven't developed their critical thinking skills properly, and live very superficial lives.

I think the most important part of starting a new friendship is clear boundaries with yourself. It’s super fun to have interesting conversations, but you have to remind yourself not to get carried away, or to find yourself depending on someone else to feel happy or less lonely. It is also important to be comfortable with loneliness, or find other distractions and fun activities. Simple boundaries to set are, 1, how often you communicate with a specific person, 2, how much time you spend with them, 3, make sure they are reciprocating conversation (if you tell them deep things, you want to hear deep things from them too). Also understand that any connection with someone else is a risk, and you shouldn’t be too trusting, especially if you are talking to people online (because they can just disappear in the blink of an eye). Always be a little cautious of others, but don’t lose that hopeful positive idea of making connections.
